scenario_stem:
Redfield Energy Drinks is a private limited company founded 6 years ago by twin sisters Priya and Nina Rao. It produces a natural mango and lime energy drink sold in 1,800 convenience stores across Country X, employing 46 full-time staff at a bottling plant. Annual revenue reached $3.6 million last year, up 8% on the previous year, and the drink holds 9% of the youth energy drink market behind two multinational rivals.

The marketing director has $120,000 for the next 12 months and must choose between sponsoring the Country X national basketball league for $100,000, with logos on courtside boards and team shirts for one season, or a six-month social media campaign costing $110,000 aimed at 18-24 year-olds. A smaller trial of the sponsorship raised brand awareness by 14% in the capital city.

questions.question_text: Define 'sponsorship'.
questions.model_answer: A business paying to support an event, team or individual in exchange for displaying its name or logo to a wide audience, gaining publicity and brand awareness [2].

knowledge_max_2: paying to associate the business name with an event, team or individual
gaining publicity and brand awareness from the association

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Redfield Energy Drinks of sponsoring the national basketball league rather than running social media adverts.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Sponsorship provides repeated exposure of the Redfield name [k] to 18-24 year-old basketball fans through courtside boards and team shirts across one season [app]. Benefit 2: Association with the national league gives the drink a healthy, energetic image [k] that appeals to the young buyers it must win over from two multinational rivals [app].

knowledge_max_2: sponsorship gives repeated, wide exposure to the brand name
association with an event or league builds a positive image
application_max_2: courtside boards and team shirts reaching fans across a season
winning young buyers from two multinational rivals

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why sponsorship may not increase sales for Redfield Energy Drinks.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: The $100,000 fee uses most of the $120,000 budget [k], leaving only $20,000 for everything else that drives purchase decisions [app], so awareness may rise without enough in-store support to convert it into sales [an]. Reason 2: Sponsorship reaches mainly basketball fans [k], a narrower audience than the 1,800 convenience stores across Country X [app], so many young buyers outside the sport never see the logo and buying habits do not change [an].

analysis_max_2: awareness may rise without converting into sales without in-store support
non-fans never see the logo so buying habits do not change

questions.question_text: Do you think Redfield Energy Drinks should sponsor the national basketball league? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The sponsorship would build positive brand awareness [k] among 18-24 year-old fans through courtside boards and shirts all season [app], helping Redfield close the gap on two multinational rivals at 9% market share [an]. However, the $110,000 social media campaign [app] would reach 18-24 year-olds precisely for six months with clicks and sales tracked directly [k], converting awareness into purchases faster [an]. Overall, Redfield should sponsor the basketball league [eval] because the 14% awareness lift shown in the trial is hard evidence rather than speculation, and an image built over a season outlasts a six-month advert run [eval].

knowledge_max_2: sponsorship builds brand awareness and positive image
social media advertising allows precise targeting and measurable results
application_max_2: courtside boards and shirts reaching 18-24 year-olds all season

evaluation_max_2: weighs trial evidence of a 14% awareness lift against social media measurability
justified recommendation to sponsor the league based on durable image and hard evidence

scenario_stem:
Marlowe & Bright Biscuits is a private limited company that has baked cream crackers and fruit biscuits in the eastern region for 9 years. It employs 58 factory staff and supplies 320 supermarkets across Country X. Annual sales revenue was $5.4 million last year, but a social media complaint about an underweight pack spread after a customer posted photos, and sales fell 11% in the last quarter. The affected batch was certified at 200g but averaged 187g.

The managing director has $25,000 to repair the company's image before the holiday season. Option one is a public relations campaign — a factory open day for 40 food retailers and journalists plus a press release, costing $16,000. Option two is a newspaper advertising campaign across 8 regional papers costing $22,000. The board also wants the pack-weight complaint investigated while the campaign runs.

questions.question_text: Define 'public relations'.
questions.model_answer: The part of marketing that builds a favourable image and goodwill with the public through unpaid coverage such as press events, open days and news stories, rather than paid advertising [2].

knowledge_max_2: building a favourable image and goodwill with the public

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Marlowe & Bright Biscuits of the public relations campaign rather than newspaper advertising.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Coverage earned through the open day and press release carries more credibility than paid advertising [k] because 40 food retailers and journalists would experience the bakery first-hand [app]. Benefit 2: The campaign costs $16,000 against $22,000 for newspapers [k], saving $6,000 while reaching the decision-makers behind 320 supermarket listings [app].

knowledge_max_2: earned coverage is more credible than paid advertising
public relations is cheaper than press advertising
application_max_2: 40 food retailers and journalists experiencing the bakery first-hand

questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Marlowe & Bright cannot control what journalists write [k] after the open day [app], so coverage could rehash the 187g pack-weight story instead of celebrating the bakery, deepening distrust rather than repairing it [an]. Drawback 2: Public relations reaches only the 40 attending retailers and journalists [k] compared with 8 regional papers [app], so most supermarket buyers never hear the company's side and sales may keep falling [an].

analysis_max_2: uncontrolled coverage could deepen distrust instead of repairing the image

questions.question_text: Do you think Marlowe & Bright Biscuits should run the public relations campaign rather than the newspaper advertising? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The PR campaign would rebuild credibility [k] by letting 40 food retailers and journalists see the bakery and the 200g pack quality first-hand [app], which could win back the 320 supermarket listings lost after an 11% fall in quarterly sales [an]. However, newspaper advertising across 8 regional papers [app] would reach far more of the public at once with a message the company fully controls [k], though at $22,000 it costs $6,000 more than the $16,000 PR option [an]. Overall, Marlowe & Bright should choose the PR campaign [eval] because trust, not awareness, is the problem this 187g batch created, so third-party voices will persuade sceptical shoppers better than paid adverts [eval].

scenario_stem:
Mango Flash Snacks is a private limited company producing baked plantain chips for 4 years, sold in 850 corner shops and school canteens across Country X. It employs 23 workers and generated $880,000 in revenue last year. Packets retail at $1.50. Owner Dani Reyes plans to launch a chilli-mango flavour aimed at 13-19 year-olds this spring and has set a target of 60,000 extra packets in the first month.

The launch budget is $45,000. Option one is a 6-week viral video campaign: a 30-second clip of friends trading Mango Flash packets costing $15,000 to produce, seeded to 4 student influencers with 2.3 million combined followers. Option two is a 3-week evening television campaign costing $40,000, expected to reach 1.1 million viewers.

questions.question_text: Define 'viral marketing'.
questions.model_answer: A promotional method where a message, usually a short video, spreads rapidly from person to person online as viewers choose to share it, giving wide reach at very low cost [2].

knowledge_max_2: a message spreads rapidly online from person to person
viewers choose to share it, giving wide reach at low cost

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Mango Flash Snacks of the viral video campaign rather than television advertising.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Viral video costs only $15,000 [k], one third of the $45,000 budget, far below the $40,000 television alternative, so the rest can fund stock and distribution [app]. Benefit 2: If viewers share the clip it spreads from person to person [k], reaching 13-19 year-olds through the 4 student influencers' 2.3 million combined followers [app].

knowledge_max_2: viral video is low cost compared with television advertising
pass-along sharing can multiply the audience exponentially
application_max_2: $15,000 versus $40,000 leaves budget for stock and distribution
reach aimed at 13-19 year-olds via 4 student influencers with 2.3 million followers

questions.question_text: Explain two risks for Mango Flash Snacks of choosing the viral video campaign.
questions.model_answer: Risk 1: Success depends on viewers choosing to share [k], so if the 30-second clip fails to engage, reach stays far below the 2.3 million influencer followers [app], and the spring target of 60,000 extra packets may be missed entirely [an]. Risk 2: A viral message can spread for the wrong reasons [k]; a clip misread as mocking students could damage the brand with exactly the 13-19 year-olds it wants to recruit [app], turning a launch into a costly public relations problem [an].

knowledge_max_2: sharing is voluntary, so reach is uncertain

application_max_2: clip may fall flat with 2.3 million influencer followers

analysis_max_2: 60,000 extra packet target may be missed entirely
a backlash would turn the launch into a public relations problem

questions.question_text: Do you think Mango Flash Snacks should run the viral video campaign? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The viral campaign would cost $15,000 [app] and its pass-along nature suits the 13-19 year-olds who live on social media [k], so a genuinely funny clip could reach far beyond the 2.3 million influencer followers at almost no extra cost [an]. However, television for $40,000 guarantees reach to 1.1 million evening viewers [app] with a message the company fully controls [k], de-risking the spring launch of the chilli-mango flavour [an]. Overall, Mango Flash should run the viral clip and bank the $25,000 saving [eval] because the target audience lives online and the saving can fund launch stock and school canteen sampling [eval].

knowledge_max_2: viral marketing suits digitally native young audiences at low cost
television advertising guarantees reach with full message control
application_max_2: $15,000 viral budget versus $40,000 television reach of 1.1 million viewers

analysis_max_2: a shareable clip could multiply reach beyond the 2.3 million followers

evaluation_max_2: weighs uncertain pass-along reach against guaranteed controlled exposure
justified recommendation to run the viral campaign and bank the $25,000 saving

scenario_stem:
Scarlet Meadow Fashion is a private limited company founded 8 years ago, designing streetwear for 18-30 year-olds. It runs 5 stores in Country X, employs 64 staff and generated $7.2 million in revenue last year. The brand won a national design award in 2024. The directors want to sell online in two neighbouring markets, Country V and Country W, where online clothing sales are growing 15% a year among 18-30 year-olds.

The marketing manager has $150,000 and must choose between one global mega-influencer campaign costing $130,000 run identically in both countries, or local campaigns costing $140,000 in total — two regional celebrities plus a launch event in each capital city. Country V buyers trust local celebrity endorsement, while Country W has stricter advertising rules requiring pre-clearance of promotional content.

questions.question_text: Define 'advertising'.
questions.model_answer: Paid-for promotion of a product or brand through media such as television, newspapers or social media, designed to inform or persuade customers to buy [2].

knowledge_max_2: paid-for promotion of a product or brand
designed to inform or persuade customers to buy

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Scarlet Meadow Fashion of the global mega-influencer campaign.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: One campaign is produced and purchased once [k], costing $130,000 to cover Country V and Country W instead of two separate local shoots [app]. Advantage 2: A single mega-influencer with a huge following gives instant, massive reach [k], building rapid awareness among the 18-30 year-olds the brand wants in both growing markets [app].

knowledge_max_2: one global campaign is cheaper and simpler than running two local campaigns
a mega-influencer gives instant, massive reach
application_max_2: $130,000 covering both Country V and Country W instead of two local shoots
fast awareness among 18-30 year-olds in both growing markets

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Scarlet Meadow Fashion of the global mega-influencer campaign.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: An identical advert ignores local differences [k]; Country V buyers trust local celebrity endorsement [app], so a foreign mega-influencer may feel irrelevant and fail to persuade them to buy [an]. Drawback 2: Country W requires pre-clearance of promotional content [k]; a global campaign shot without local approval could be rejected or banned there [app], wasting most of the $130,000 before a single online sale is made [an].

knowledge_max_2: a standardised campaign ignores local preferences and culture

analysis_max_2: the foreign face may fail to persuade Country V buyers to purchase

questions.question_text: Do you think Scarlet Meadow Fashion should run the global mega-influencer campaign or the two local campaigns? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The global campaign would cost $130,000 [app] and give one consistent brand message across both markets [k], saving $10,000 against the local option and simplifying management [an]. However, the local campaigns at $140,000 [app] use trusted regional celebrities and launch events [k], matching Country V's preference for local faces and clearing Country W's pre-clearance rules, which should convert awareness into faster online sales [an]. Overall, Scarlet Meadow should run the two local campaigns [eval] because the extra $10,000 buys legal certainty in Country W and credibility in Country V, the two barriers most likely to block a $7.2 million brand breaking into these markets [eval].

knowledge_max_2: a global campaign gives a consistent message across markets at lower cost
local campaigns match local tastes and legal rules
application_max_2: $130,000 global campaign versus $140,000 local campaigns
regional celebrities and launch events matching Country V and clearing Country W rules
analysis_max_2: the global option saves $10,000 and simplifies management
local campaigns should convert awareness into faster online sales
evaluation_max_2: weighs $10,000 saving and consistency against legal certainty and local credibility
justified recommendation to run the two local campaigns

scenario_stem:
Alderwick Preserves Co is a partnership of two brothers, Theo and Jonah Marchetti, making rose-hip and quince jams by hand since 2015. It sells 95,000 jars a year at $6.40 each, generating $608,000 in revenue, and employs 19 staff in the Lakeside region. Domestic jam sales have grown only 2% in 2 years, and two supermarket chains demanded a 12% price discount last month.

A distributor in neighbouring Country V offers to stock 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 per jar if Alderwick meets Country V food-safety labelling within 6 months, with the contract running for 3 years. Exporting would add $24,000 in freight and require $9,000 of new certification. The brothers must decide whether to start exporting to Country V.

questions.question_text: Define 'export'.
questions.model_answer: Selling goods produced in one country to customers in another country, extending a business's market beyond its domestic borders [2].

knowledge_max_2: selling goods produced in the home country to overseas customers
extending the market beyond domestic borders

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Alderwick Preserves Co of exporting to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: The order would add sales beyond the stagnant domestic market [k] — 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 is about $153,000 of new revenue [app]. Opportunity 2: Entering Country V spreads risk [k], so if two domestic supermarket chains force the 12% discount, the brothers still have a second market to sell into [app].

knowledge_max_2: exporting adds sales beyond the domestic market
selling into a second country spreads risk
application_max_2: 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 is about $153,000 of new revenue
a second market cushions the 12% discount demanded by supermarket chains

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Alderwick Preserves Co of exporting to Country V.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The brothers must meet Country V food-safety labelling within 6 months [k], so failure would waste the $9,000 certification fee before a single jar ships [app], delaying entry and straining the Lakeside factory's cash flow [an]. Problem 2: Freight adds $24,000 a year [k] and the $5.10 jar price is $1.30 below the domestic $6.40 [app], squeezing margins so the order may add little profit even when the factory is full [an].

$5.10 export price versus $6.40 domestic, plus $24,000 freight
analysis_max_2: failure to certify wastes the fee and strains cash flow

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderwick Preserves Co should start exporting to Country V? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting would open a Country V market while domestic sales crawl at 2% [k], with 30,000 jars a year at $5.10 worth about $153,000 even after $24,000 freight — roughly $129,000 before certification [app]. However, the $5.10 price is $1.30 below domestic $6.40 [app] and the $9,000 certification carries a real risk of rejection within 6 months [k], so refusal would waste the fee and six months of planning [an], while the domestic slide continues unchecked [an]. Overall, Alderwick should accept the export order [eval] because a second market reduces dependence on supermarkets demanding 12% discounts, and the numbers still add up after certification [eval].

knowledge_max_2: exporting opens overseas markets when domestic demand stagnates

analysis_max_2: roughly $129,000 remains before certification
rejected paperwork would waste the $9,000 certification fee
evaluation_max_2: weighs overseas growth and reduced supermarket dependence against price and certification risk
justified recommendation to export because the numbers work after costs

scenario_stem:
Halloran Cycle Works is a private limited company founded 10 years ago by Sofia Lindqvist, producing electric cargo bicycles for delivery riders. It employs 72 workers, generated $9.8 million in revenue last year and sells each bike at $4,100, with domestic demand now flat. Country W, where e-bike deliveries grew 22% last year, has no domestic producer and the boom is driven by courier firms switching from vans to cargo bikes.

The board wants to enter Country W and must choose between a joint venture with Weidler Logistics, a local company with 40 depots, costing $1.2 million for a 50% share, or building its own assembly plant in Country W for $3.5 million. Country W also charges a 12% tariff on imported bicycles, ruling out simple exporting.

Opportunity 2: Sharing the $1.2 million cost means half the capital at risk [k] instead of $3.5 million for its own plant, preserving cash for product development [app].

knowledge_max_2: a joint venture provides local knowledge and distribution channels

questions.model_answer: Problem 1: A 12% tariff on imported bicycles [k] makes shipping finished bikes from Country X costly [app], raising the retail price and dampening demand among cost-conscious delivery riders [an]. Problem 2: Sharing a joint venture halves control [k]; Halloran must agree every major decision with Weidler Logistics [app], risking slow decisions and erosion of the 10-year brand it built on technical quality [an].

questions.model_answer: The joint venture would halve the capital at risk — $1.2 million for 50% [app] — and bring instant local knowledge [k] through Weidler's 40 depots [app], letting Halloran enter the 22% growth market quickly before Weidler's rivals move [an]. However, building its own plant for $3.5 million keeps full control and all the profits [k], while a partner might push its own fleet priorities and erode Halloran's 10-year brand reputation [an]. Overall, Halloran should choose the joint venture [eval] because with a 12% import tariff ruling out simple exporting, shared risk and local expertise are worth more than owning every profit [eval].

scenario_stem:
Fernwell Skincare is a private limited company producing a shea-butter hand cream since 2017. It sells 260,000 tubes a year at $8.50 across 140 pharmacies in Country X, generating $2.21 million in revenue, and employs 33 staff. The cream won a national beauty award in 2024 and its golden packaging is instantly recognisable. Enquiries from Country S surged after a beauty blogger featured the cream in a video watched 900,000 times.

The directors must choose between exporting directly from Country X, requiring $70,000 of export set-up and shipping documentation for each shipment, or licensing the cream to Country S maker Bellano Cosmetics, which would produce and sell locally for 7% royalties on sales. Forecast sales in Country S are 120,000 tubes a year at $8.00 per tube.

questions.question_text: Define 'licensing'.
questions.model_answer: Giving another business permission to produce or sell your product in return for a fee or royalty, usually a percentage of their sales [2].

knowledge_max_2: granting another business the right to produce or sell your product
in return for a fee or a royalty, usually a percentage of sales

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities for Fernwell Skincare of licensing the cream to Bellano Cosmetics.

Opportunity 2: Bellano knows Country S labelling and retail networks [k], so the cream can reach buyers immediately, earning 7% royalties on forecast sales of 120,000 tubes a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: licensing avoids the capital cost of direct exporting

application_max_2: no $70,000 set-up or shipping documentation needed for Country S

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Fernwell Skincare of licensing the cream to Bellano Cosmetics.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: Fernwell loses control over quality [k]; if Bellano dilutes the formula to cut costs, the shea-butter hand cream's reputation built since 2017 could collapse in both markets [app], destroying the brand image with loyal buyers [an]. Drawback 2: Royalties of 7% [k] yield only $67,200 a year on sales of 120,000 tubes at $8.00 [app], far below the margin Fernwell earns on its own 260,000 tubes, limiting the upside of going overseas [an].

royalties are a small share of overseas sales value
application_max_2: dilution risk to the shea-butter formula and its 2017 reputation
7% of 120,000 tubes at $8.00 yields about $67,200 a year
analysis_max_2: brand damage would hit loyal buyers in both markets
the royalty stream limits the financial upside of overseas expansion

questions.question_text: Do you think Fernwell Skincare should license the cream to Bellano Cosmetics rather than export directly? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Licensing would give Fernwell entry to Country S without the $70,000 export set-up [app] and instant access to Bellano's local knowledge [k], turning interest from a 900,000-view video into steady royalty income on 120,000 tubes a year [an]. However, 7% royalties yield only about $67,200 a year [app] and Fernwell would surrender control of quality and brand [k], risking the hand-cream image built since 2017 if Bellano cuts corners [an]. Overall, Fernwell should license rather than export directly [eval] because the low upfront risk suits a first foreign market, and once Country S sales prove themselves Fernwell can renegotiate rates or open its own route [eval].

quality-control loss could damage the brand if Bellano cuts corners
evaluation_max_2: weighs low-risk royalty income against lost control and lower returns
justified recommendation to license first, with the option to renegotiate later

scenario_stem:
Tarrow Tandoor is a private limited company operating 7 tandoor restaurants across Country X, employing 96 staff and generating $3.1 million in revenue last year. Country X sales grew 9% last year, and it imports most spice blends from three suppliers. Two investors in neighbouring Country Z have asked to open Tarrow-branded restaurants there, where 2 million residents have no tandoor restaurant and imported spice blends cost 15% more than in Country X.

The board must choose between international franchises — each franchisee pays a $35,000 set-up fee plus 5% of annual sales — or one company-owned restaurant in Country Z costing $420,000. Franchisees would handle staffing, local advertising and daily operations, while a company-owned outlet would keep all profits but need two Country X managers relocating for 2 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'franchise'.

knowledge_max_2: franchisor sells the right to trade under its brand name
franchisee pays fees and must follow agreed operating standards

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages to Tarrow Tandoor of the international franchise option.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Franchises need no $420,000 capital outlay [k]; two franchisees would pay $35,000 each plus 5% of sales, giving Tarrow brand presence in Country Z with minimal investment [app]. Advantage 2: Local franchisees understand Country Z's market and staffing [k], so Tarrow can open two restaurants faster than relocating two managers for 2 years [app].

knowledge_max_2: franchising expands with little capital investment by the franchisor

application_max_2: two franchisees paying $35,000 each plus 5% of sales instead of $420,000

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Tarrow Tandoor of international franchising into Country Z.

Drawback 2: Quality control is harder at a distance [k]; poor spicing or service from a franchisee in Country Z would tarnish the Tarrow name built across 7 restaurants [app], risking complaints that travel back to Country X [an].

knowledge_max_2: franchisors retain only a small share of outlet profits

questions.question_text: Do you think Tarrow Tandoor should expand into Country Z through international franchises? Justify your answer.

scenario_stem:
Willowmere Spices is a private limited company blending mild curry pastes and dried herbs since 2011. It sells 480,000 jars a year at $4.20, generating $2.016 million in revenue, and employs 41 staff across its kitchen, warehouse and office. It won 2 national food awards in 2025. Export orders to Country Z now total 60,000 jars a year and are growing 30% annually. Two Country Z supermarkets have already agreed to trial the range.

Country Z buyers prefer milder, low-salt pastes, halal-certified ingredients and labels in the local language. Reformulating and re-labelling for Country Z would cost $95,000. Keeping the standard range saves the $95,000 but the importer warns sales could fall by 25% — about 15,000 jars a year — within 12 months.

scenario_stem:
Bramble & Vine Chocolatiers is a private limited company founded 12 years ago, making single-origin dark chocolate bars sold through 12 boutique shops in Country X. It employs 38 staff and generated $5.6 million in revenue last year. Two department-store buyers in Country S and Country T ask for 150,000 bars a year combined, and Country S customs inspect chocolate imports slowly.

The board is choosing between licensing a Country S confectioner to produce Bramble & Vine bars there for 6% royalties on wholesale sales, or franchising its boutique shop concept to a Country S retail partner for a $50,000 entry fee plus 4% of shop sales. Franchising would cost $80,000 to recruit and train franchisees over 6 months; licensing requires no shop investment.

Benefit 2: Franchising keeps the shop experience and brand story under tighter control [k], reinforcing the brand image customers pay $5.6 million a year for [app].
